section.paragraph: To motivate the precise definition of a limit, let’s consider the function
Intuitively, it is clear that when $$x$$ is close to $$3$$ but $$x \neq 3$$ , then $$f(x)$$ is close to $$5$$ , and so $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 3}f(x) = 5$$ .
To obtain more detailed information about how $$f(x)$$ varies when $$x$$ is close to $$3$$ , we ask the following question:

list.item: How close to $$3$$ does $$x$$ have to be so that $$f(x)$$ differs from $$5$$ by less than $$0.1$$ ?

section.paragraph: The distance from $$x$$ to $$3$$ is $$|x - 3|$$ and the distance from $$f(x)$$ to $$5$$ is $$\left| f(x) - 5 \right|$$ , so our problem is to find a number $$\delta$$ (the Greek letter delta) such that
If $$\left| x - 3 \middle| > 0 \right.$$ , then $$x \neq 3$$ , so an equivalent formulation of our problem is to find a number $$\delta$$ such that
Thus an answer to the problem is given by $$\delta = 0.05$$ ; that is, if $$x$$ is within a distance of $$0.05$$ from $$3$$ , then $$f(x)$$ will be within a distance of $$0.1$$ from $$5$$ .

If we change the number $$0.1$$ in our problem to the smaller number $$0.01$$ , then by using the same method we find that $$f(x)$$ will differ from $$5$$ by less than $$0.01$$ provided that $$x$$ differs from $$3$$ by less than $$(0.01) \slash 2 = 0.005$$ :

The numbers $$0.1$$ , $$0.01$$ , and $$0.001$$ that we have considered are error tolerances that we might allow. For $$5$$ to be the precise limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$3$$ , we must not only be able to bring the difference between $$f(x)$$ and $$5$$ below each of these three numbers; we must be able to bring it below any positive number. And, by the same reasoning, we can! If we write $$\varepsilon$$ (the Greek letter epsilon) for an arbitrary positive number, then we find as before that

note.title: Precise Definition of a Limit
note.heading: Precise Definition of a Limit
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function defined on some open interval that contains the number $$a$$ , except possibly at $$a$$ itself. Then we say that the limit of $$\mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x} \right)$$ as $$\mathbf{x}$$ approaches $$\mathbf{a}$$ is $$\mathbf{L}$$ , and we write
if for every number $$\varepsilon > 0$$ there is a number $$\delta > 0$$ such that

section.paragraph: It is traditional to use the Greek letters $$\varepsilon$$ and $$\delta$$ in the precise definition of a limit.

Since $$|x - a|$$ is the distance from $$x$$ to $$a$$ and $$\left| f(x) - L \right|$$ is the distance from $$f(x)$$ to $$L$$ , and since $$\varepsilon$$ can be arbitrarily small, the definition of a limit can be expressed in words as follows:

list.item: $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ means that the distance between $$f(x)$$ and $$L$$ can be made arbitrarily small by requiring that the distance from $$x$$ to $$a$$ be sufficiently small (but not $$0$$ ).
$$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ means that the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close as we please to $$L$$ by requiring $$x$$ to be close enough to $$a$$ (but not equal to $$a$$ ).

section.paragraph: We can also reformulate Definition 2 in terms of intervals by observing that the inequality $$\left| x - a \middle| < \delta \right.$$ is equivalent to $$- \delta < x - a < \delta$$ , which in turn can be written as $$a - \delta < x < a + \delta$$ . Also $$\left. 0 < \middle| x - a \right|$$ is true if and only if $$x - a \neq 0$$ , that is, $$x \neq a$$ . Similarly, the inequality $$\left| f(x) - L \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ is equivalent to the pair of inequalities $$L - \varepsilon < f(x) < L + \varepsilon$$ . Therefore, in terms of intervals, Definition 2 can be stated as follows:

list.item: $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ means that for every $$\varepsilon > 0$$ (no matter how small $$\varepsilon$$ is) we can find $$\delta > 0$$ such that if $$x$$ lies in the open interval $$\left( {a - \delta,a + \delta} \right)$$ and $$x \neq a$$ , then $$f(x)$$ lies in the open interval $$\left( {L - \varepsilon,L + \varepsilon} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: We interpret this statement geometrically by representing a function by an arrow diagram as in Figure 2, where $$f$$ maps a subset of $$\mathbb{R}$$ onto another subset of $$\mathbb{R}$$ .

example.paragraph: Although we chose $$\delta = 0.08$$ , any smaller positive value of $$\delta$$ would also have worked.

section.paragraph: The graphical procedure used in Example 1 gives an illustration of the definition for $$\varepsilon = 0.2$$ , but it does not prove that the limit is equal to $$2$$ . A proof has to provide a $$\delta$$ for every $$\varepsilon$$ .

In proving limit statements it may be helpful to think of the definition of limit as a challenge. First it challenges you with a number $$\varepsilon$$ . Then you must be able to produce a suitable $$\delta$$ . You have to be able to do this for every $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , not just a particular $$\varepsilon$$ .

Imagine a contest between two people, $$A$$ and $$B$$ , and imagine yourself to be $$B$$ . Person $$A$$ stipulates that the fixed number $$L$$ should be approximated by the values of $$f(x)$$ to within a degree of accuracy $$\varepsilon$$ (say, $$0.01$$ ). Person $$B$$ then responds by finding a number $$\delta$$ such that if $$\left. 0 < \middle| x - a \middle| < \delta \right.$$ , then $$\left| f(x) - L \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ . Then $$A$$ may become more exacting and challenge $$B$$ with a smaller value of $$\varepsilon$$ (say, $$0.0001$$ ). Again $$B$$ has to respond by finding a corresponding $$\delta$$ . Usually the smaller the value of $$\varepsilon$$ , the smaller the corresponding value of $$\delta$$ must be. If $$B$$ always wins, no matter how small $$A$$ makes $$\varepsilon$$ , then $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ .

example.heading: Example 2

list.item: Preliminary analysis of the problem (guessing a value for $$\delta$$ ). Let $$\varepsilon$$ be a given positive number. We want to find a number $$\delta$$ such that $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| \left( {4x - 5} \right) - 7 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ But $$\left| (4x - 5) - 7 \middle| = \middle| 4x - 12 \middle| = \middle| 4(x - 3) \middle| = 4 \middle| x - 3 \right|$$ . Therefore we want $$\delta$$ such that $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left. 4 \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ that is, $${{if} 0 < |x - 3| < \delta} {then} {|x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{4}}$$ This suggests that we should choose $$\delta = \varepsilon \slash 4$$ .

Proof (showing that this $$\delta$$ works). Given $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , choose $$\delta = \varepsilon \slash 4$$ . If $$\left. 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right.$$ , then $$|(4x - 5) - 7| = |4x - 12| = 4|x - 3| < 4\delta = 4\left( \frac{\varepsilon}{4} \right) = \varepsilon$$

section.paragraph: Note that in the solution of Example 2 there were two stages—guessing and proving. We made a preliminary analysis that enabled us to guess a value for $$\delta$$ . But then in the second stage we had to go back and prove in a careful, logical fashion that we had made a correct guess. This procedure is typical of much of mathematics. Sometimes it is necessary to first make an intelligent guess about the answer to a problem and then prove that the guess is correct.

list.item: Guessing a value for $$\delta$$ . Let $$\varepsilon > 0$$ be given. We have to find a number $$\delta > 0$$ such that $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| x^{2} - 9 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ To connect $$\left| x^{2} - 9 \right|$$ with $$|x - 3|$$ we write $$\left| x^{2} - 9 \middle| = \middle| \left( {x + 3} \right)\left( {x - 3} \right) \right|$$ . Then we want $$\left. {if} 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right. {then} \left| x + 3 \middle| \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ Notice that if we can find a positive constant $$C$$ such that $$\left| x + 3 \middle| < C \right.$$ , then $$\left| x + 3 \middle| \middle| x - 3 \middle| < C \middle| x - 3 \right|$$ and we can make $$\left. C \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \right.$$ by taking $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \slash C \right.$$ , so we could choose $$\delta = \varepsilon \slash C$$ . We can find such a number $$C$$ if we restrict $$x$$ to lie in some interval centered at $$3$$ . In fact, since we are interested only in values of $$x$$ that are close to $$3$$ , it is reasonable to assume that $$x$$ is within a distance $$1$$ from $$3$$ , that is, $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < 1 \right.$$ . Then $$2 < x < 4$$ , so $$5 < x + 3 < 7$$ . Thus we have $$\left| x + 3 \middle| < 7 \right.$$ , and so $$C = 7$$ is a suitable choice for the constant. But now there are two restrictions on $$|x - 3|$$ , namely $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < 1 \right.$$ and $$|x - 3| < \frac{\varepsilon}{C} = \frac{\varepsilon}{7}$$ To make sure that both of these inequalities are satisfied, we take $$\delta$$ to be the smaller of the two numbers $$1$$ and $$\varepsilon \slash 7$$ . The notation for this is $$\delta = \min\left\{ {1,\varepsilon \slash 7} \right\}$$ .

Showing that this $$\delta$$ works. Given $$\varepsilon > 0$$ , let $$\delta = \min\left\{ {1,\varepsilon \slash 7} \right\}$$ . If $$\left. 0 < \middle| x - 3 \middle| < \delta \right.$$ , then $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < 1\Rightarrow 2 < x < 4\Rightarrow \middle| x + 3 \middle| < 7 \right.$$ (as in part 1). We also have $$\left| x - 3 \middle| < \varepsilon \slash 7 \right.$$ , so $$|x^{2} - 9| = |x + 3||x - 3| < 7 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{7} = \varepsilon$$ This shows that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{2} = 9$$ .

section.heading: The Limit Laws
section.paragraph: As the preceding examples show, it is not always easy to prove that limit statements are true using the $$\varepsilon$$ , $$\delta$$ definition. In fact, if we had been given a more complicated function such as $$f{(x)} = {({6x^{2} - 8x + 9})} \slash {({2x^{2} - 1})}$$ , a proof would require a great deal of ingenuity. Fortunately this is unnecessary because the Limit Laws stated in Section 2.3 can be proved using Definition 2, and then the limits of complicated functions can be found rigorously from the Limit Laws without resorting to the definition directly.

image.alt: Details A vertical line, a curve, a horizontal line, and two vertical segments are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The positive x axis is displayed with tick marks a minus delta, a, and a + delta, in the order from left to right. The negative y axis is displayed with tick mark N, below the origin. A vertical line extends downward in the fourth quadrant from tick mark a. The curve has two parts. The first part goes up and to the right from the third quadrant, concave down, reaches its high point in the first quadrant, goes down and to the right, approaches x = a, and exits very closely to the left of x = a. The second part enters the fourth quadrant, very close to the right of x = a, goes up and to the right, concave down, and continues to go upward to the right in the first quadrant. A horizontal line y = N is drawn from the third quadrant to the fourth quadrant crosses the negative y axis at tick mark N, and intersects the curve at two points. Vertical line segments extend downward from tick marks a minus delta and a + delta until they reach the horizontal line y = N.
